title: Final Case Study: The Campus Merch Shop
setup:
import pandas as pd
customers = pd.read_csv("customers.csv")
products = pd.read_csv("products.csv")
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
explanation: You've been hired as the data analyst for a small campus merch shop. Three tables are ready: customers (who shops), products (what's for sale) and orders (who bought what, and how many). Each order links a customer_id to a product_id. No new tools here: combine everything you've learned to answer real business questions. Read each question slowly, decide which tables you need, then build your answer one step at a time.

example.code: orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id").merge(products, on="product_id").assign(revenue=lambda d: d["quantity"] * d["price"])[["name", "product", "revenue"]].head()

lines.explain: Add the customer's details to each order.
Who bought what, and for how much.

tasks.prompt: The owner asks: how many items sold in each product category? Biggest first.

solution_lines.explain: Link each order to its product.

tasks.prompt: Which products have never been ordered? Show just the product name.
hints: Left join products to orders, then look for missing order_id.
m = products.merge(orders, on="product_id", how="left"), then m[m["order_id"].isna()][["product"]]

solution_lines.explain: No matching order: Poster and Mug.

tasks.prompt: Show each city's total revenue (quantity × price), keeping only cities with $100 or more.
tasks.answer:
r = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id").merge(products, on="product_id").assign(revenue=lambda d: d["quantity"] * d["price"]).groupby("city")["revenue"].sum()
r[r >= 100]
hints: Merge all three tables, add revenue, group by city and sum. Then filter the result like a column.

solution_lines.explain: Boston 203, Hartford 100, New Haven 100. Providence's Hugo never ordered.

tasks.prompt: Draw a bar chart of total revenue per customer, biggest first.
hints: Same chain as before, but group by name, sort, then plot.

solution_lines.explain: Dev, Finn and Ava are the top customers.

tasks.prompt: Final challenge: label each customer a "Big Spender" (spent $80 or more) or "Regular". Show the label for each customer name.
tasks.answer:
totals = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id").merge(products, on="product_id").assign(revenue=lambda d: d["quantity"] * d["price"]).groupby("name")["revenue"].sum()
totals.apply(lambda s: "Big Spender" if s >= 80 else "Regular")
hints: Work out each customer's total first. Then apply a lambda with if/else: "Big Spender" if s >= 80 else "Regular".
totals = ... .groupby("name")["revenue"].sum(), then totals.apply(lambda s: "Big Spender" if s >= 80 else "Regular")

solution_lines.line: totals.apply(lambda s: "Big Spender" if s >= 80 else "Regular")
solution_lines.explain: A one-line if/else for every customer: Dev and Finn are Big Spenders.

recap: You did a real analyst's job: joined three tables, found missing data, summarised and filtered groups, drew a chart and labelled customers. That's everyday Python data analysis. Congratulations on finishing the course! 🎉
